Let
\[
I=a_0a_4-4a_1a_3+3a_2^2
\]
and
\[
J=a_0a_2a_4-a_0a_3^2-a_1^2a_4+2a_1a_2a_3-a_2^3.
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{Z(R)=k[I,J]}.
\]

**Solution**

The defining relations say exactly that \(R=U(\mathfrak g)\), where
\[
\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2\ltimes V
\]
and \(V=\langle a_0,\dots,a_4\rangle\) is abelian, with \(V\) the irreducible \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\)-module of highest weight \(4\). The action is
\[
[H,a_i]=(4-2i)a_i,\qquad [E,a_i]=i a_{i-1},\qquad [F,a_i]=(4-i)a_{i+1}.
\]

First check that \(I,J\) are central. Since the \(a_i\) commute pairwise, it is enough to check commutation with \(E,F,H\). For \(I\),
\[
[E,I]=0,\qquad [F,I]=0,\qquad [H,I]=0,
\]
because
\[
[E,a_0a_4-4a_1a_3+3a_2^2]
=4a_0a_3-4(a_0a_3+3a_1a_2)+12a_1a_2=0,
\]
and similarly
\[
[F,I]=4a_1a_4-4(3a_2a_3+a_1a_4)+12a_2a_3=0.
\]
The \(H\)-weights also cancel termwise. A direct application of the same derivations gives
\[
[E,J]=[F,J]=[H,J]=0.
\]
Thus \(k[I,J]\subseteq Z(R)\).

It remains to prove that there are no other central elements. Give \(R=U(\mathfrak g)\) its PBW filtration. If \(z\in Z(R)\), then its leading symbol \(\operatorname{gr} z\in S(\mathfrak g)\) is invariant under the adjoint action of \(\mathfrak g\).

We claim
\[
S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}=S(V)^{\mathfrak{sl}_2}.
\]
Indeed, write \(\mathfrak g^*=\mathfrak{sl}_2^*\oplus V^*\). For a generic \(\lambda\in V^*\), the stabilizer of \(\lambda\) in \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) is zero. For example, over an algebraic closure, the binary quartic \(x^4+y^4\) has no nonzero infinitesimal \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\)-stabilizer. Hence the \(V\)-coadjoint action translates the whole \(\mathfrak{sl}_2^*\)-fiber over such a \(\lambda\). Therefore any \(\mathfrak g\)-invariant polynomial on \(\mathfrak g^*\) is independent of the \(\mathfrak{sl}_2^*\)-coordinates. What remains is precisely an \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\)-invariant polynomial in \(a_0,\dots,a_4\).

So every central element has leading term in \(S(V)^{\mathfrak{sl}_2}\). The invariant ring of the irreducible binary quartic module is
\[
S(V)^{\mathfrak{sl}_2}=k[I,J].
\]
For completeness, one can verify this from the character
\[
\operatorname{ch} S(V)=
\prod_{m=-2}^{2}(1-tx^{2m})^{-1}.
\]
The multiplicity of the trivial representation in degree \(d\) is the coefficient of \(x^0\) minus the coefficient of \(x^2\), giving Hilbert series
\[
\sum_{d\ge0}\dim S^d(V)^{\mathfrak{sl}_2}t^d
=\frac1{(1-t^2)(1-t^3)}.
\]
Since \(I\) and \(J\) are algebraically independent of degrees \(2\) and \(3\), they generate all invariants.

Now take \(z\in Z(R)\). Its leading symbol is some polynomial \(P(I,J)\). Since \(P(I,J)\) itself is central in \(R\), subtracting it from \(z\) lowers the PBW degree. Induction on PBW degree gives \(z\in k[I,J]\).

Therefore
\[
\boxed{
Z(R)=k\!\left[
a_0a_4-4a_1a_3+3a_2^2,\,
a_0a_2a_4-a_0a_3^2-a_1^2a_4+2a_1a_2a_3-a_2^3
\right].
}
\]
